metadata.title: Civic Education Outcomes After Emergency Lockdowns: International Evidence from the COVID-19 Pandemic

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses ICCS 2016 and ICCS 2022 Grade 8 student data from 14 countries plus one benchmarking participant (Germany’s North Rhine-Westphalia). ICCS employs a stratified two-stage cluster design (schools selected with probability proportional to size, then classrooms sampled), and the authors state that all analyses apply sampling weights; in pooled analyses, senate weights are used so each country contributes equally. Standard errors are computed using jackknife repeated replication (JRR), which is consistent with the complex survey design. The manuscript does not describe any additional ML-specific preprocessing that would require weight omission; instead, the reported associations are estimated with sampling weights and design-based variance estimation.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analysis is restricted to countries/participants that participated in both ICCS 2016 and ICCS 2022. The dependent variables come from ICCS Grade 8 civic outcomes: civic knowledge (cognitive test with four content domains) and linked scales for trust and expected participation in protest and politics. The study uses the full available ICCS sample within these participating countries/participant, applying ICCS sampling weights; for missing dependent-variable information, the authors use casewise deletion, while for independent variables they use a missing-category approach for categorical variables and a separate code (999) plus an indicator for continuous variables.

main_findings.dataset_used: ICCS 2016 & 2022 Grade 8 Civic Knowledge (civic institutions/systems, principles, participation, roles & identities)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Separate weighted regressions with jackknife repeated replication; standardized interaction coefficients (Table 3a): Avg. Stringency = −0.035*** (SE 0.010); Days Closed = −0.041*** (SE 0.011).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICCS 2016 & 2022 Grade 8 Civic Knowledge the study leveraged student demographics (gender, age, immigrant status) and socioeconomic background controls together with country-level participation/exclusion rates and COVID-19 severity indicators to estimate how changes in civic knowledge between 2016 and 2022 varied with lockdown stringency or school-closure duration, finding that greater lockdown stringency and longer school closures were associated with larger declines in civic knowledge (standardized coefficients −0.035*** and −0.041***, respectively). This indicates that stronger and longer COVID-19 restrictions—especially those reducing in-person schooling—may have undermined civic learning for secondary students, suggesting that post-lockdown civic-education catch-up and continuity planning should be prioritized, though the design is not a causal experiment.

main_findings.dataset_used: ICCS 2016 & 2022 Grade 8 Trust in civic institutions (INTRUST scale)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Table 3a standardized interaction coefficients: Avg. Stringency = −0.057*** (SE 0.011); Days Closed = −0.076*** (SE 0.012).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICCS 2016 & 2022 Grade 8 Trust in civic institutions the study leveraged student background controls and country-level participation/exclusion and COVID-19 severity indicators to model how within-country changes in trust varied with lockdown stringency or school-closure duration, finding that both higher stringency and longer closures were associated with larger declines in trust (standardized coefficients −0.057*** and −0.076***). This indicates that prolonged or more stringent pandemic restrictions may have eroded students’ trust in civic institutions, implying that education systems and policymakers should incorporate civic trust-supportive activities (e.g., transparent communication and civic dialogue) into recovery strategies, while noting that causal claims are limited by the observational, repeated-cross-section design.

main_findings.dataset_used: ICCS 2016 & 2022 Grade 8 Expected participation in legal protest activities (LEGACT scale)
main_findings.target_variable: Expected participation in legal protest activities (LEGACT)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Table 3a standardized interaction coefficients: Avg. Stringency = 0.087*** (SE 0.010); Days Closed = 0.031*** (SE 0.008).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICCS 2016 & 2022 Grade 8 Expected participation in legal protest activities the study leveraged student background controls and country-level participation/exclusion and COVID-19 severity indicators to estimate how changes in expected legal protest participation varied with lockdown stringency or school-closure duration, finding that higher lockdown stringency and longer closures were associated with increases in expected legal protest participation (standardized coefficients 0.087*** and 0.031***). This indicates that more restrictive pandemic contexts may have motivated some students to expect greater civic voice through lawful protest channels, suggesting that civic education during and after crises should address constructive participation pathways, while recognizing that the study measures expectations rather than actual behavior.

main_findings.dataset_used: ICCS 2016 & 2022 Grade 8 Expected participation in illegal protest activities (ILLACT scale)
main_findings.target_variable: Expected participation in illegal protest activities (ILLACT)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Table 3a standardized interaction coefficients: Avg. Stringency = 0.041*** (SE 0.010); Days Closed = 0.034*** (SE 0.009).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICCS 2016 & 2022 Grade 8 Expected participation in illegal protest activities the study leveraged student demographics and socioeconomic background controls plus country-level participation/exclusion and COVID-19 severity indicators to estimate how changes in expected illegal protest participation varied with lockdown stringency or school-closure duration, finding that both higher stringency and longer closures were associated with increases (or smaller declines) in expected illegal protest participation (standardized coefficients 0.041*** and 0.034***). This indicates that more stringent pandemic restrictions may have shifted students’ expected civic engagement toward protest-oriented behavior, implying that policymakers should pair crisis restrictions with civic education that emphasizes lawful, democratic participation and conflict-resolution skills, while avoiding causal interpretations.

main_findings.dataset_used: ICCS 2016 & 2022 Grade 8 Expected electoral participation (ELECPART scale)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Table 3b standardized interaction coefficients: Avg. Stringency = 0.006 (SE 0.009, not significant); Days Closed = −0.024** (SE 0.009).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICCS 2016 & 2022 Grade 8 Expected electoral participation the study leveraged student background controls and country-level participation/exclusion and COVID-19 severity indicators to estimate how changes in expected electoral participation varied with lockdown stringency or school-closure duration, finding no significant association with average lockdown stringency (0.006) but a negative association with school-closure duration (−0.024**). This indicates that longer school closures may have weakened students’ expectations of electoral participation, suggesting that recovery civic curricula should explicitly support understanding of elections and democratic representation after disruptions, while noting that the paper reports associations rather than causal effects.

main_findings.dataset_used: ICCS 2016 & 2022 Grade 8 Expected active political participation (POLPART scale)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Table 3b standardized interaction coefficients: Avg. Stringency = 0.048*** (SE 0.010); Days Closed = 0.026** (SE 0.010).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICCS 2016 & 2022 Grade 8 Expected active political participation the study leveraged student background controls and country-level participation/exclusion and COVID-19 severity indicators to estimate how changes in expected active political participation varied with lockdown stringency or school-closure duration, finding positive associations for both measures (standardized coefficients 0.048*** for average stringency and 0.026** for days closed). This indicates that more stringent or longer pandemic restrictions may have increased students’ expectations of conventional political engagement (e.g., party/organization involvement), implying that civic education should channel heightened political interest into democratic, institutional participation, while recognizing the observational nature of the evidence.

data.outcome_summary: The study links ICCS 2016 and ICCS 2022 Grade 8 civic outcomes with national COVID-19 containment measures from OxCGRT (school-closure duration and an average stringency index) for 14 countries plus Germany’s North Rhine-Westphalia. Civic knowledge is estimated using ICCS plausible values and combined across five PVs using Rubin’s rules, while trust and expected participation outcomes are ICCS linked scales. The authors estimate separate weighted regression models (sampling weights: senate weights; variance: jackknife repeated replication) and report standardized interaction coefficients rather than ML prediction metrics. Across outcomes, greater lockdown stringency and longer school closures are associated with larger declines in civic knowledge and trust in civic institutions, while they are associated with increases (or smaller declines) in expected protest participation (legal and illegal) and expected active political participation. Expected electoral participation shows inconsistent results, with no significant association for stringency but a negative association for closure duration. Limitations include a small number of countries, observational identification (no causal design), and measurement error from linking scales across cycles.
